slides.eyebrow: IB Mathematics: Applications and Interpretations HL · Unit 5 · Lesson 4
slides.title: Logistic models
slides.lede: Online lesson: one story, six scenes

slides.title: A Promising Start
slides.alt: The phone from the lesson, drawn large: it fills as residents adopt smartphones

setup.preamble: Smartphones have just gone on sale in a small region. Shops stock them, and the first owners show them off to friends.
setup.para: A survey taken at launch, which we call $t=0$, finds that $5\%$ of residents own a smartphone. A second survey two years later, at $t=2$, finds that $10\%$ own one. Time $t$ is measured in years.

facts.html: $t$ is measured in years since launch

scene.alt: A phone that fills with adoption beside the graph of adoption against time

slides.title: A model that doubles
slides.stem: If adoption keeps doubling every two years, what model could we use?

walk.cap: Let $E(t)$ be the percentage: start at $5$, double every $2$ years

scene.alt: A phone that fills with adoption beside the graph of adoption against time

slides.title: Four years on
slides.stem: Predict: what does the model give after four years?

walk.cap: Two more years doubles it again
walk.note: Adding $5$ again would give $15\%$. Doubling gives $20\%$.

scene.alt: A phone that fills with adoption beside the graph of adoption against time

slides.title: Follow the Model
slides.alt: The phone from the lesson, drawn large: it fills as residents adopt smartphones

setup.preamble: The region's planners want to know how many phones to expect. They trust the doubling model from the first scene.
setup.para: Their forecast is $E(t)=5\cdot 2^{t/2}$, the percentage of residents with a smartphone after $t$ years. A region cannot have more owners than residents, so a full region is $100\%$.

scene.alt: A phone that fills with adoption beside the graph of adoption against time

slides.title: Six years and eight years
slides.stem: Follow the model forward. What does it predict after six years? After eight years?

scene.alt: A phone that fills with adoption beside the graph of adoption against time

slides.title: Ten years on
slides.stem: Predict: what does the model give after ten years?

walk.cap: Two more years doubles it again
walk.note: That is more than all of the residents. A market share cannot exceed $100\%$ of the population.

scene.alt: A phone that fills with adoption beside the graph of adoption against time

slides.title: The calculation or the assumption?
slides.stem: What has failed: the calculation, or our assumption?
choices: The assumption that adoption can keep doubling

walk.note: Doubling for ever needs more than $100\%$ of the residents.

scene.alt: A phone that fills with adoption beside the graph of adoption against time

slides.title: What Should Happen?
slides.alt: The phone from the lesson, drawn large: it fills as residents adopt smartphones

setup.preamble: The forecast passed $100\%$, which cannot happen. Before choosing a new formula, think about how adoption really spreads.
setup.para: We return to the same region and follow it for longer. What we knew still holds: $5\%$ owned a phone at launch, $10\%$ two years later, and never more than $100\%$ of residents can own one. The doubling forecast stays on the graph, faded.

scene.alt: A phone that fills with adoption beside the graph of adoption against time

slides.title: Who is left to adopt?
slides.stem: As more residents adopt, what happens to the number still available to adopt? Describe in words how adoption should continue.

walk.note: Every new owner leaves one fewer resident who could still adopt, so new adopters get harder to find.

scene.alt: A phone that fills with adoption beside the graph of adoption against time

slides.title: Later readings
slides.stem: More readings arrive from the same region. Describe what they show.

walk.note: Adoption keeps rising, but it is slowing down.

scene.alt: A phone that fills with adoption beside the graph of adoption against time

slides.title: Must it reach 100%?
slides.stem: Must the eventual level of adoption be $100\%$?

blocks.text: Some residents may never adopt due to cost, access, preference.

walk.note: Suppose adoption levels off at $80\%$. There is no equation yet, only the behaviour we need: early growth, then slowing towards a ceiling.

scene.alt: A phone that fills with adoption beside the graph of adoption against time

slides.title: Meet the Logistic
slides.alt: The phone from the lesson, drawn large: it fills as residents adopt smartphones

setup.preamble: The later readings rose and then slowed. A logistic model does that: it grows like the doubling forecast at first, then levels off.
setup.para: A logistic model has the form $P(t)=\dfrac{L}{1+Ae^{-kt}}$, with three unknowns: the limit $L$, a constant $A$, and the growth rate $k$. We take $L=80$, the ceiling proposed in the last scene. Then two readings, $5\%$ at $t=0$ and $10\%$ at $t=2$, fix $A$ and $k$.

facts.html: Limit $L=80$: the ceiling from the last scene

scene.alt: A phone that fills with adoption beside the graph of adoption against time

slides.title: Find A and k (1 of 2)
slides.stem: Take $L=80$, the ceiling from the last scene. Use the two readings to find $A$ and $k$ in $P(t)=\frac{L}{1+Ae^{-kt}}$.

scene.alt: A phone that fills with adoption beside the graph of adoption against time

slides.title: Find A and k (2 of 2)
slides.stem: Take $L=80$, the ceiling from the last scene. Use the two readings to find $A$ and $k$ in $P(t)=\frac{L}{1+Ae^{-kt}}$.

walk.note: When $L$ is not known, enter the data in the GDC and use logistic regression: it finds $L$, $A$ and $k$ together.

scene.alt: A phone that fills with adoption beside the graph of adoption against time

slides.title: Check against later readings
slides.stem: The model used only two readings. Does it agree with the later readings, $32\%$ at $t=6$ and $60\%$ at $t=10$?

walk.note: Built from two readings, the model still matches the later ones.

scene.alt: A phone that fills with adoption beside the graph of adoption against time

slides.title: What the exponential term does
slides.stem: Predict: as $t$ increases, what happens to $e^{-0.381t}$?

walk.note: $y=80$ is a horizontal asymptote: adoption nears $80\%$, never reaching it.

scene.alt: A phone that fills with adoption beside the graph of adoption against time

slides.eyebrow: Meet the logistic · Trace the models
slides.title: Where do the predictions separate?
Where Is It Fastest?
slides.alt: The phone from the lesson, drawn large: it fills as residents adopt smartphones

slides.eyebrow: Where is it fastest? · The situation
slides.title: Planning for the busiest years

setup.preamble: The planners now trust a model that levels off. Next they want to know when the region changes fastest, so shops and networks are ready.
setup.para: Adoption in the region follows $P(t)=\dfrac{80}{1+15e^{-0.381t}}$, with $t$ in years since launch. The model levels off at $80\%$.

scene.alt: A phone that fills with adoption beside the graph of adoption against time

slides.title: Compare equal intervals (1 of 2)
slides.stem: Predict: does adoption grow fastest at the beginning, near the ceiling, or somewhere in between?

scene.alt: A phone that fills with adoption beside the graph of adoption against time

slides.title: Compare equal intervals (2 of 2)
slides.stem: Predict: does adoption grow fastest at the beginning, near the ceiling, or somewhere in between?

walk.note: The biggest rise is between $t=6$ and $t=8$, in the middle.

scene.alt: A phone that fills with adoption beside the graph of adoption against time

slides.title: The inflection point (1 of 2)
slides.stem: Where is the steepest point, the inflection point? Give the level of adoption and the time.

walk.note: The inflection point is at half the limit.

scene.alt: A phone that fills with adoption beside the graph of adoption against time

slides.title: The inflection point (2 of 2)
slides.stem: Where is the steepest point, the inflection point? Give the level of adoption and the time.

scene.alt: A phone that fills with adoption beside the graph of adoption against time

slides.title: Is adoption falling?
slides.stem: After the inflection point, is adoption falling?
choices: No, it still rises, but more slowly
No, it rises at the same rate

walk.note: The total keeps rising. What shrinks is the number of new adopters each year.

scene.alt: A phone that fills with adoption beside the graph of adoption against time

slides.title: Explore and Judge
slides.alt: The phone from the lesson, drawn large: it fills as residents adopt smartphones

setup.preamble: The region will soon weigh some proposals. First, see what each part of the model controls.
setup.para: A logistic model of this kind has three settings. The growth rate $k$ sets how quickly adoption rises, the limit $L$ is the level it settles towards, and the start is the percentage at $t=0$. For our region, $k\approx 0.38$, $L=80$, and the start is $5\%$.

scene.alt: A phone that fills with adoption beside the graph of adoption against time

slides.title: Two proposals for the region
slides.stem: The region is considering two different actions. Read both carefully before matching them to a change in the model.

walk.note: The government pays part of the price of every phone. Residents who would have waited buy sooner, and some who could never afford one can now buy.
Smartphones reach the region earlier, so adoption has been under way for longer. At $t=0$, more residents already own a phone than the $5\%$ in our story.

scene.alt: A phone that fills with adoption beside the graph of adoption against time

slides.title: Subsidy or earlier launch?
slides.stem: Which change to the model could represent the subsidy? Which could represent the earlier launch?

walk.cap: A subsidy: cheaper phones, faster adoption
A subsidy: more residents can afford one
An earlier launch: the region starts further along

scene.alt: A phone that fills with adoption beside the graph of adoption against time

slides.title: Why logistic? What could fail?
slides.stem: Why is a logistic model more plausible here? What could still make its forecast fail?

tex: &\text{Growth slows as fewer residents are left}

walk.note: The $80\%$ limit and the growth rate are assumptions. Prices or new technology could change them.

scene.alt: A phone that fills with adoption beside the graph of adoption against time

slides.eyebrow: Beyond the story · Logistic growth around us
slides.title: Where else does it happen?

items.title: Yeast in sugar water
what: The number of yeast cells in a bottle of warm sugar water
Tracked through the height of the foam they make
why: Cells divide quickly while sugar is plentiful
The sugar runs low and waste builds up
The population levels off at what the bottle can support
exp: Set up
Mix 250 mL warm water and 2 tbsp sugar in a clear bottle
Stir in 1 teaspoon of dried yeast
Tape a ruler to the side; cover the top loosely
Every 15 minutes for 3 hours, read the foam height
Record time and height in a table
Plot height against time

items.title: Duckweed on a tray of water
what: The number of duckweed fronds floating on a tray of pond water
why: Every frond buds new fronds
As the surface fills, fronds crowd and shade each other
Growth slows towards the number the tray can hold
exp: Set up
Fill a shallow tray with pond water
Add 5 fronds and place the tray by a window
Each day at the same time
Photograph the tray from directly above
Count the fronds on the photo
Continue for about three weeks
Plot the count against days

items.title: Bean seedling height
what: The height of a bean plant, day by day from planting
why: A seedling grows slowly at first
It grows fastest in the middle of its growth
It slows as it nears the height its species can reach
exp: Plant five beans in separate pots on a windowsill
Each day at the same time
Measure each stem from soil to tip
Record the five heights
Find the mean height for each day
After six weeks, plot mean height against days

items.title: Fish in a stocked pond
what: The number of fish after a pond is stocked with a few
why: With food and space to spare, numbers climb quickly
Crowding and a limited food supply then slow growth
The population settles near what the pond can support
exp: Practise mark and recapture on a bowl of dried beans
Mark 20 beans and mix them back in
Draw a handful and count the marked ones
Estimate the total
$\text{total}\approx 20\times \text{handful}\div\text{marked}$
Repeat monthly on a real pond, with its keeper's help
Plot the estimates against months

items.title: Flu in a school
what: The total number of people who have caught flu since the first case
why: Early on, each sick student meets many healthy ones
Later, most people have already had it
New cases fall away, so the total levels off
exp: Set up the game
Give one student a card
Everyone else starts without one
Each round
Each card holder taps one random classmate
They take a card if they have none
Count the card holders after each round
Stop when it levels off; plot count against round

items.title: Streaming subscribers
what: The total number of paying subscribers to a new streaming service
why: Word of mouth speeds growth at first
Eventually most people who would subscribe already have
The total flattens
exp: Find published data
Open the company's quarterly reports
Note totals for 8 to 12 quarters from launch
Record quarter number and total in a table
Plot subscribers against quarter
Mark where the curve bends from speeding up to slowing down

items.title: Electric cars on the road
what: The share of cars that are electric
why: A few early adopters go first
The share climbs quickly as prices fall and chargers spread
It slows as the market fills
exp: Once a month, same day and time
Tally 100 cars in the school car park
Count how many are electric
Work out the percentage
After a year, plot percentage against months
Compare with national figures from a transport statistics website

items.title: A viral video's views
what: The total views of a new video, day by day
why: Each viewer may share it, so views surge
Most people who would watch it soon have
New views dry up and the total levels off
exp: Choose a video posted today
Each day at the same time
Note the total view count
Work out the new views since yesterday
Continue for two weeks
Plot total views against days
Mark the day with the most new views

items.title: A rumour in a class
what: The number of students who have heard a harmless piece of news
why: Each student who knows tells friends, so it spreads faster and faster
Later, few students are left who have not heard
The count levels off
exp: In the morning, tell one student a harmless message
At each break
Ask everyone who knows it to raise a hand
Count the hands
Record the time and the count
Plot the count against the time of day
